title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
prompt: Given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid`, return the length of the shortest clear path from the top-left cell `(0, 0)` to the bottom-right cell `(n-1, n-1)`. A clear path only passes through cells with value `0`, and you may move in any of the 8 directions (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally) to an adjacent cell. The length of a path is the number of visited cells. If no such path exists, or the start or end cell is not `0`, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Moving diagonally from (0,0) directly to (1,1) gives a path of length 2.
The path (0,0) -> (0,1) -> (0,2) -> (1,2) -> (2,2) has length 5, but a shorter one using diagonals exists with length 4.
The only cell, which must serve as both start and end, is blocked, so no path can exist at all.

hints: Because all moves cost the same (one step), the shortest path in an unweighted grid is found with BFS, not DFS.
Unlike the classic 4-directional flood fill, this problem allows all 8 neighboring directions (including diagonals) — update your neighbor list accordingly.

Check the start and end cells are 0 up front as an early exit, mark cells visited as soon as they're enqueued (not when dequeued) to avoid enqueuing the same cell multiple times, and track path length as the BFS depth plus one.

solution.approach: Since every move has the same cost, BFS explores cells in strictly increasing order of path length, so the first time the bottom-right cell is reached is guaranteed to be via a shortest path. Run BFS from (0,0) using all 8 directions, marking a cell visited the moment it's enqueued (to avoid redundant work), and track the path length as the number of cells visited so far. Return -1 if the queue empties without ever reaching the target.
